met-436535.note: Painted at Saint-Rémy in 1889. The wheat and the sky move to the same brush rhythm, and the cypress goes up like a flame.

met-435809.note: One of a series of paintings of the seasons, made in 1565. The reapers cut wheat while a few rest in the shade; the whole valley is in the picture.

met-437881.note: A woman holds a window casement open with one hand and a pitcher with the other. Nothing happens; the light carries it.

met-437879.note: A tronie: a character study, not a commissioned portrait. The sitter is unidentified.

met-436947.note: The boat is cut off by the frame and the river fills the background with no horizon, a composition often compared to Japanese prints.

met-12116.note: The Generalife is the garden beside the Alhambra in Granada. Sargent used wax crayon with the wash: the wax resists the paint and leaves the white lights.

met-12127.note: Shown at the 1884 Paris Salon, where it caused a scandal. Sargent had painted the right shoulder strap fallen and later painted it back in place.

met-437397.note: Painted at 54, four years after bankruptcy forced the sale of his house and collection.

met-435882.note: The apples carry the composition. The table edge and the pot tilt because Cézanne painted from more than one viewpoint at once.

met-435868.note: One of five paintings of the subject from the early 1890s. Two men face each other across a table in a silence the picture treats as its subject.

met-435876.note: Hortense Fiquet, Cézanne's wife, sat for him many times. The armchair and the dress get the same attention as the face.

met-436121.note: The woman sits at the edge of the canvas while the flowers take the centre. A portrait that looks away from its sitter.

met-436173.note: Late Degas: pastel built up in layers of hatching until the colour vibrates.

met-438817.note: A rehearsal room at the Paris Opéra. The ballet master Jules Perrot stands at the right, leaning on his cane, while the girls stretch and wait.

met-10154.note: Bierstadt travelled with Frederick Lander's survey expedition to the Rockies in 1859 and painted this in his New York studio four years later.

met-11122.note: A man lies on a dismasted boat among sharks, with a waterspout on the horizon. Homer reworked it by 1906.

met-11145.note: A farmer in shirtsleeves cuts wheat with a scythe, his army jacket on the ground. Painted in 1865, the year the Civil War ended.

met-10481.note: In 1859 Church showed this alone in a New York studio and charged admission. Visitors brought opera glasses to study the detail.

met-437854.note: Painted in the mid-1840s, near the end of Turner's life. The ships and whales are barely more solid than the light around them.

met-437097.note: From a set of four paintings of the seasons that Millet made for a private patron.

met-438816.note: The Met dates it ca. 1846–67: Rousseau kept returning to the canvas for roughly two decades.

met-39799.note: From the series Thirty-six Views of Mount Fuji. Fuji is the small peak in the distance; the subject is the wave.

met-282040.note: Early photographic materials were so sensitive to blue light that skies usually printed as blank white. Clouds that register at all are an achievement.

met-337499.note: A Swiss lake in watercolour, made in 1843 on Turner's late tours. The colour does the work that line would do in his earlier drawings.

met-337491.note: A drawing for its own sake. Rembrandt walked the country around Amsterdam and set down what he saw in a few strokes of pen and wash.

met-459092.note: The Jas de Bouffan was the Cézanne family estate near Aix-en-Provence. He painted its trees and buildings for years.

met-336327.note: Made in 1889, the same year as Wheat Field with Cypresses, inside the asylum at Saint-Rémy where Van Gogh had admitted himself.

met-459238.note: Rembrandt varied his ink from pale to near-black, pushing the cottage forward and the wood back.

met-544184.note: A pharaoh of the Twelfth Dynasty. The heavy lids and lined face depart from the smooth ideal of earlier royal portraits.

met-547031.note: Egyptian blue is one of the earliest synthetic pigments, made by heating sand with copper and calcium minerals.

met-313330.note: Jadeite is carved by abrasion: slowly, with sand and cord. A pendant like this took many hours of work.

met-38435.note: A kinnari is half bird, half woman, a celestial musician in Indian literature. Gold set with garnet.

met-327104.note: The Met cannot say whether this is a king or a god. The headdress and the pose fit either.

met-459086.note: De Hooch composes with doorways and tiled floors: each opening leads to another lit space.

met-359362.note: A monotype: oil colour painted on a plate and pressed onto paper once. Degas made his landscapes from memory, in the studio.

met-682931.note: A mezzotint is made by roughening the whole plate, then scraping light back in. It suits clouds.

pg-walden-deliberately.title: Where I Lived, and What I Lived For
pg-walden-deliberately.creator: Henry David Thoreau
pg-walden-deliberately.note: Thoreau lived at Walden Pond from 1845 to 1847. This is the passage the book is remembered for.

pg-walden-stream.title: Where I Lived, and What I Lived For
pg-walden-stream.creator: Henry David Thoreau
pg-walden-stream.note: From the same chapter. Time as a stream to fish in, and the sky as its deeper water.

pg-whitman-spider.title: A Noiseless Patient Spider
pg-whitman-spider.creator: Walt Whitman
pg-whitman-spider.note: One image across two stanzas: the spider pays out thread into empty space, and so does the soul. The line itself repeats "filament" three times, like thread leaving the spinneret.

pg-whitman-grass.title: Song of Myself, 6
pg-whitman-grass.creator: Walt Whitman
pg-whitman-grass.note: The first of several guesses at what grass is. He never settles on one.

pg-emerson-eyeball.title: Nature, I
pg-emerson-eyeball.creator: Ralph Waldo Emerson
pg-emerson-eyeball.note: The "transparent eye-ball" became Emerson's most quoted and most caricatured image.

pg-emerson-child.title: Nature, I
pg-emerson-child.creator: Ralph Waldo Emerson
pg-emerson-child.note: Few adults see nature; a child does. Emerson's test for a lover of nature: inner and outer senses still adjusted to each other.

pg-melville-ishmael.title: Loomings
pg-melville-ishmael.creator: Herman Melville
pg-melville-ishmael.note: The opening paragraph. Ishmael's cure for gloom is the sea.

pg-dickinson-hope.title: "Hope" is the thing with feathers
pg-dickinson-hope.creator: Emily Dickinson
pg-dickinson-hope.note: Dickinson published almost nothing in her lifetime. Two stanzas, one bird.

pg-dickinson-nobody.title: I'm nobody! Who are you?
pg-dickinson-nobody.creator: Emily Dickinson
pg-dickinson-nobody.note: First published after her death. The frog is the other half of the joke.
